newsitem.title: SPAIN: Microsoft downplays network computer threat.
newsitem.headline: Microsoft downplays network computer threat.

text.p: Microsoft Corp. Chairman Bill Gates Thursday shrugged off suggestions that new network computers posed a lasting threat to the giant software producer.

Gates, in Madrid for a conference on Internet users, predicted that the smaller network computers would prove too slow and inflexible to overtake personal computers, the main platform for Microsoft's operating system software.
"We see the PC going forward," Gates told a news conference. "If you look at the market share the network computer has today, that's what we predict for the future."
His forecast flies in the face of what some other industry leaders have seen as a bright new market niche.

The network computer is basically a stripped-down personal computer meant to provide easy, cheap access to the Internet and internal corporate computer networks that does not need the Windows operating system.
The machines have limited memory and no add-ons such as disk drives, but use software that sits on a host computer known as a server.
Larry Ellison, chairman of rival software producer Oracle Corp., which first publicised the idea for the machines, has said he expects "explosive" growth for network computers.
Oracle has said the machines' inexpensive make-up and replacement cost and could make the PC obsolete.
IBM, which introduced its version called Network Station in September, said it would buoy all of its businesses, including hardware, services and software.
But Gates dismissed these claims, saying the network computers would end up frustrating users because they would be slowed down by having to use software on already clogged networks.
"Unlike the direction in PC technology where the trend is for faster and faster access, the network computer actually makes it slower for them on the server," he said.

He said a better response for cheap access to the Internet's World Wide Web was to provide slim-line software -- like Microsoft's NetPC -- to allow people to use smaller PCs and still run applications.
"Network computer is throwing away all software. Clearly Microsoft doesn't think people want to do that," Gates said.
Gates said that in its aim for simplicity Microsoft was moving to scale down its Windows NT software and make it easy and convenient for e-mail, file-sharing and Web access.
